passages.text: And with that said, I would like to hand it over to our moderator for this session,
Josh McLetter, who is the Senior Advisor for Media and Internet Freedom at USAID. Over to you, Josh.
Thank you so much, Cheyenne. Good morning, good evening. Thanks for those of you who've logged
on to spend an hour with us today. Some of you joined us last month for the first of this series
in which we launched USAID's Disinformation Primer, a handbook produced by the DRG Center
to help you when you are designing your programming to address the issue of disinformation.
So last month's webinar, we talked about basic terms and concepts around what constitutes
disinformation and how it works. And in this webinar, we're attempting to respond to the big
and important questions from the last webinar that so many of you asked. What can USAID do to
counter disinformation? And this is a big question, and it's going to differ by the kind of context
you work in. But for today, we're going to attempt to give you a glimpse into some of the more
widespread programs that USAID has been supporting to counter disinformation and build more resilient
information systems in the countries where we work. This is just going to be a glimpse. We hope
to pack in a lot of information into an information-rich hour. Again, I want to advise
you to take a look at the Disinformation Primer, which we feel has a lot of information and references
to even more information. And just a word about the types of interventions we're going to talk
about today. For each of these interventions, there are bodies of research that are growing daily
about new ways to counter disinformation and to refine existing approaches. And we're still
very much in the phase of learning what really works. So first and foremost, we approach all
this work with a sense of humility, though I do think that we're going to boast a little bit about
the kind of great work we can do. But we do know that we don't know enough, and there is so much
to learn. And so we are constantly in a phase of experimentation. But we do approach this with a
data-driven and evidence-based mindset. It's such a challenging problem to solve
when disinformation is so destructive and chaotic, and the costs for making it and putting it out
are really low. And at the same time, the things that we want, which is good information,
social harmony, making democracy work, the costs for that are really high. Those are some really
hard and lofty goals. But we have a couple of factors working in our favor, and I think that
our presenters are going to talk about that. And one, people really want to know the truth, and at
the end of the day, they don't like being lied to. Two, right now we work with a lot of social media
platforms where the disinformation spreads, and they're built upon an architecture in which
disinformation diffuses and spreads fast and far, but haven't yet been sufficiently incentivized
to change the way they work. And that's not a foregone conclusion. That could all change
if we make it. And three, there are so many brilliant minds studying this phenomenon and
learning more about it. So we're in a better place than we were just a few years ago on this problem.
And I would even say that the fact alone that we're talking about this as much as we do and are
concerned and are increasingly growing aware as a society is a good indicator that we're moving
in the right direction on this issue. So I want to introduce four of our colleagues from USAID,
all of whom have been involved in groundbreaking work around the issue around this, around the world
to counter disinformation in their programming. And each one of them is going to be an advocate
making the case for a certain type of approach, and they're going to give you their pitches.
After the pitches, you're going to vote for the one that you like the most, and you'll have an
opportunity to go a little deeper. And I'm going to quickly introduce them and tell you what they're
going to talk about. We're first going to hear from Shannon McGuire from the Europe Eurasia Bureau,
who's going to be the advocate for media literacy. And then we're going to hear from Jerry Porta
from USAID Philippines, who will talk about fact-checking and investigative journalism.
After that, you're going to hear from Amy Malesa from OTI, who's going to talk about
platform accountability. And then you'll hear from Adam Kaplan, also from OTI,
who will talk about messaging campaigns. So please, give them all your close attention,
and they're going to be very short, and they're going to make the hard sell. And then you will
be asked to make a vote on the approach that you think is the most important or relevant
for the disinformation problem that you might be working on. And then you'll have a chance to go
to a breakout group to learn more from them and talk to them about their approaches.
So first up, Shannon McGuire.
Great. Thank you, Josh. So I'm going to be talking about media literacy. So what is media
literacy? Media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and participate with
media in all its forms. Media literacy also builds an understanding of the role of media
in society and a healthy democracy. Why is it important? It has real-world consequences. Think
of Pizzagate, vaccine hesitancy, the events on January 6th, violence in Myanmar and India,
climate change denialists. It's very serious. Who needs media literacy? Everyone. Young people,
old people, dogs, cats, journalists, government officials, everyone.
Now I'm going to talk briefly about inoculation theory. So it's a little bit easier to contextualize
what media literacy is through an example. So the title of this webinar is called the
Other Epidemic. In other words, we're not just facing a pandemic from COVID-19,
but also from the information pollution and media manipulation around it.
So let's think of media literacy through the lens of inoculation theory. In 1961,
William J. McGuire came up with the idea of inoculation theory in response to a situation
where the goal is to persuade someone not to be persuaded by another's argument. The theory is
a model for building resistance to persuasion attempts by exposing people to arguments against
their beliefs and then giving them counter arguments to refute the attacks. In other words,
the approach works like a vaccine, which teaches your body to recognize specific dangerous pathogens
so your immune system is prepared to fight off that infection in the future.
So how does it work? First, identify the source of messages that are resonating with different
audiences that might be vulnerable to certain messages. Take, for example, the men are witches
theory. Men are witches. Okay. So we know that men are witches. They can have children well
into their 80s. They can walk down the street and not get cat called. It's like they're invisible.
They never get cold and they get paid for the same work. They get paid more for the same work that
women do. So for those who might be prey to the conspiracy that men are not witches, which is
crazy, you would say, you'd say, listen, we know that you don't follow the men are not witches
conspiracy theory. And we know you don't think you need to overthrow the patriarchy. We know that you
don't have those attitudes, but people just like you have been persuaded by these kinds of arguments
in the past. That's the first step. You make them think that their beliefs and attitudes are not
as set in stone as they think they are. Then you say, well, listen, there's a group out there
who's going to tell you that men in fact are not witches and they should be allowed to make more
money for the same job, get cheaper haircuts than women. And they shouldn't have to wait in line
for the bathroom. You introduce them to these arguments, and then you step away. Research
shows that a few things happen. First, the individual will counter, counter argue against
the propaganda more. Second, they'll be angrier at men. Third, they'll perceive men and the group
advocating for their rights to be less credible. And most importantly, they'll say they have less
intention to support the group in any way, whether it's ideologically, monetarily, or with armed
support. So wrapping all of this up, final points. We need to reimagine media literacy for the
internet hellscape that we occupy. Media literacy is not victim blaming, it's victim empowering.
Media literacy is a silver bullet if it's done right. Short-term, long-term, formal, informal,
across all age groups. Is it a cure, a proven solution? Not exactly, but just like vaccines,
it's a tool to recognize invaders and protect us. So join my breakout room for more media literacy
approaches, evidence that it works, and what to do next. Thank you. Wow, that's quite compelling,
Shannon. Men are witches. Next, we're going to hear from Jerry, who's going to talk about
investigative journalism and fact-checking. Thank you very much, Josh. We have seen disinformation
disrupting political processes and undermining people's faith in democratic systems in young
and old democracies alike. Disinformation also serves as a pretext for authoritarian leaders
to restrict freedom of information and the people's right to know, criminalizing media work
or shutting down the internet under the guise of combating fake news. Disinformation online has
major consequences offline. It can literally kill, for example, by triggering electoral violence or
by influencing people towards not protecting their health in a time of pandemic. While
disinformation has most likely always been part of political processes, albeit known by other names,
its volume has exponentially increased since the emergence of social media.
I claim the dubious distinction of working in the country that Facebook Policy Director Katie Harbath
referred to as patient zero when it comes to the weaponization of social media to spread
disinformation. The attributes that make social media a great equalizer in terms of empowering
people to potentially reach a vast audience at relatively little cost and enable a hyper-connected
society are the very same characteristics that malign influences, foreign and local, exploit to
advance propaganda, incite hate, and whitewash horrific transgressions of basic rights.
In the lead-up to the 2016 presidential elections in the Philippines, certain political actors
effectively employed individuals to surreptitiously shape online opinions, intentionally providing
misleading information for political gain, smearing the political opposition, and intimidating
others with different political views. Although a holistic response to disinformation requires a
battery of options that include the topics we are discussing today, fact-checking presents the most
direct and immediate response to disinformation. Contextually, fact-checking addresses disinformation
when it is at its most harmful, when it is propaganda, when it is dishonest, when it causes
hate and violence, and when it endangers informed choices. I think more than just the skills of
critical thinking, which other practices also promote, fact-checking is at its heart an exercise
of speaking truth to power. It is about holding institutions accountable, it is about deterring
disinformation, and encouraging an environment of critical information consumption. Fact-checking,
in particular, is very important as a resource for people actively searching for the true version of
affairs, and as a tool that is part of what we use when we encourage critical thinking. We need to
be able to point to a variety of reliable and trusted fact-checking organizations so that people
have somewhere to go when they see information they are not sure about and decide to take the
step of checking. Fact-checking goes hand in hand with the practice of investigative journalism
to ensure a more consistent supply of fact-based information, particularly content on issues of
public interest. Fact-based information is the foil to disinformation. Equally as important, investigative
journalism can be your tool to unmask networks of malicious disinformation actors, the purveyors of
deception and confusion. Let me end with a call to action. We need to be mindful of both the supply
and demand sides of fact-checking. It is vital that we work with both information producers and
consumers to strengthen the understanding of what disinformation is, as well as to identify it and
engage with social media platforms and or third-party fact-checkers to reduce its prevalence.
Fact-checking is everybody's responsibility. Join us in our breakout room so we can learn from each
other's experience and benefit from that. Thank you. Thank you, Jerry. And what's not to love in that?
A healthy fact-based information ecosystem, which is a key to democracy.
Okay, next we're going to hear from Amy talking about platform accountability.
All right. Awesome, guys. Thank you so much for joining us today and hope to see you in our breakout.
Speaking of social media and our responsibility, let's have some real talk about platform
accountability. So platform accountability has a direct impact on your work, and today I'm going
to show you how and I'm going to learn from you. Calls are increasing from civil society,
from journalists, government, and the public to hold platforms more accountable
for their share of the disinformation problem. So which platforms are we talking about here?
We're talking about the global tech platforms like Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, but also the
smaller blogs and websites where disinformation can be equally bad, if not worse. We're talking
about the dark corners of the web. So anywhere you see what we call user-generated content,
UGC, content that is generated by us as everyday citizens, members of the public.
So there's a growing understanding that platforms were designed to maximize for attention,
engagement, and emotional reactions, not accurate reporting, plural debate,
nor reasoned thinking, all the things that we love. What is platform accountability? Platform
accountability is our responsibility to define clear standards for tech companies and hold them
accountable to those standards. What does this look like in practice? Let's dig in. There are
currently five efforts that are under consideration to hold platforms more accountable. They include
number one, working with platforms themselves to provide greater transparency on how their
algorithms and ad targeting actually works behind the scenes. Number two, working with
civil society organizations to monitor complaints from users and how those complaints are handled
in line with our community standards. Number three, working with journalists to follow
internationally recognized standards for fact-checking to both label content and provide
more context around that reporting. Number four, working with government to design new legislation
to regulate how platforms moderate content at scale on their sites. And number five,
working across platforms, civil society, journalists, and government to develop consensus
around how to govern platforms together collaboratively and transparently.
So why does your voice in this moment matter? Given their widespread adoption,
these platforms will continue to directly impact our work for the foreseeable future. Platforms do
not, and they recognize this, have the staffing footprint to solve this problem alone. This is why
engagement by USAID staff and partners, especially from field missions, is so critical today. There's
a lively debate happening right now that we can engage in about how platforms should be governed
in the future, either through state governance, self-regulation, or co-governance. The key tension
is how do we balance regulation of these platforms alongside the freedoms that we hold dear and near
to our hearts, like freedom of expression, freedom of association. So have you all seen The Social
Dilemma on Netflix? Did it concern you? If it did, then this is the group for you. If you haven't, go
check it out, but please still join us today. We want to hear your voice. So come shape our approach
at USAID to how we work with platforms on the inside, but also pressure them from the outside
to change. Hope to see you in our breakout. Thanks. Thanks, Amy, and what a great message. The platforms
don't have to be this way, but we have to be the ones to change it. So next, Adam Kaplan,
who's going to talk about messaging. Thank you, Josh, and thank you to the compelling arguments
presented by my colleagues. However, central to their arguments is the idea that this
disinformation genie can be put back in the bottle, or at least constrained in a
larger bottle. That the profit interests of social media platforms and the political benefits
of politicians' lives sold over those platforms can be overcome. That the fact-checkers will be
able to keep up with the content produced by those who would seek to deceive. The technology will
stand still long enough for our audiences to be able to learn how to discern what is real or not,
to know when they're being manipulated, and to do so in spite of AI deepfake enhancements.
And that we as consumers can overcome our lower brainstem instincts not to be emotionally charged
by content scientifically engineered and robustly tested on us to make us react emotionally.
I contend that all of these efforts are absolutely necessary and still stand a very real chance
of not being enough. The COVID epidemic has surfaced at the truly wicked nature of this
problem. And I additionally contend that the ability of our democratic societies to function
hangs in the balance. What does civil discourse and our ability to resolve conflicts amicably
look like when we cannot agree on sufficient facts to define our mutual conditions?
If we cannot reestablish the currency of facts and truth, at least for a polarity of us,
then fact-based democratic decision-making is in deep, deep trouble. For this reason,
I suggest we need to find a new way to negotiate our divergent worldviews. We need to find
something on which we can agree. And increasingly in experiments in deliberative democracy are
surfacing that we can come together, absent labels and political parties, over our deeply held values.
The approach I'm recommending is that we find a way through any and all communication vehicles
to attempt to build cohesion on what we value and where we want our societies to go.
I invite you to come with me on an exploration of what this content might look like,
explore what we can do with it, and to create and inspire cohesion and find new common ground.
Adam, thank you. I love this idea of taking down the temperature a little bit and, you know,
getting people working together and to foster deliberative democracy. This is a great idea.
So, my colleagues, you've heard four compelling, well-crafted arguments for different kinds of
approaches, and you have about one minute now to vote for the one that resonates the most for you.
Just to recap, Shannon talked about media literacy, Jerry talked about fact-checking
and investigative journalism, Amy talked about platform accountability,
and Adam talked about messaging campaigns. So, please find in the right-hand margin
the polls in which you can register your vote. Thank you so much, Josh. And again,
just reiterating, you could go ahead and click on the activities tab, which is the triangle,
square, and circle, and then you'll be able to click on polls and vote. Right now, we do have
some folks voting. We're just waiting on a couple more votes there, and I will display the results
now. And as we continue voting, you'll just see the differences. Awesome. All right, I'll just
keep the poll open, but it seems like we have majority of our votes. Back to you, Josh.
Great. Well, thank you all for voting in a transparent and democratic fashion. Cheyenne
Nix is going to drop some links for you to head into a breakout session to talk more with our
advocates. And you'll have about 15 minutes to learn more about their approach, ask questions.
Each room that you join will have a rapporteur who's going to take some notes and do a readout
summary to the rest of the group after to make a closing case for their different approach.
Yes. Okay. Great. So, welcome back, everyone. I hope you all had thoughtful and productive,
albeit brief, discussions with our speakers and our colleagues. We will have
rapporteurs from each breakout session to give us a summary of what they talked about,
and you'll have another opportunity to vote afterwards as they make the closing arguments
about their approaches. So, first, I'm going to introduce Diana Parzyk from the DRG Center,
who's going to make the closing argument for media literacy. Thanks, Diana.
Thanks, Josh, and thanks, Shannon. So, just to wrap up our session, we did talk about the five
myths that we were busted regarding media literacy, the first being that media literacy
only teaches critical thinking skills, and it does not. It also teaches the role of media
serving as a watchdog and the importance of media literacy as it relates to the health of democracy.
The second myth that we busted in our session was media literacy is mainly taught in schools as part
of civic education, and according to the research that's out there, media literacy is needed for
everyone, so not just in, you know, with civil society and academics and within the school
systems, but also it's needed in government and the importance related to that. The third myth
that we discussed was media literacy, that it takes too long, but we discussed in our session
that media literacy needs both a short and long-term approach, and the research that's
currently out there showed immediate results, which leads into our fourth myth, that there's
no evidence to support media literacy works, and we discussed recent RANDS research in which
within a couple minutes that far right and far left individuals, hard-to-reach individuals,
were easily persuaded and changed their behaviors after learning some media literacy
approaches to no longer like Kremlin disinformation tactics. The fifth myth that we discussed
was media literacy is a silver bullet, and it's not. We all talked about how media literacy needs
to be done in a collective approach with other approaches to counter disinformation,
and then the last thing, we did have a question in our group specifically related to
the trust in media after implementing media literacy sort of programs, and we talked
a little bit about how youth have generally less trust in media. So that's a wrap for
our group and media literacy, and I hope everyone votes for us. Thanks. I'll turn over to the next one.
Yeah, thanks, Diana, and thanks for letting us know about the myths. I think that there's a saying that
if you will it, it's not a myth, so hey, maybe we can have more media literacy, and next we're going
to hear from Lorian Miles from the DRG Center who's going to make the closing argument on
fact-checking and investigative journalism. Thanks, Lori. Thanks, Josh. So we had a fabulous
conversation that really focused on what are the advantages of going with fact-checking and
investigative journalism, and as you heard in the opening arguments, fact-checking presents
the most direct and immediate response to disinformation, and it is at its heart an
exercise of speaking truth to power. It's about holding institutions accountable, and so what's
great about fact-checking and investigative journalism is it can graft right into our
existing programming. In our breakout session, we really focused on the supply side and thinking
through how journalism and journalists can incorporate fact-checking into their existing
work to better detect and debunk the disinformation, and so standing up permanent bodies like a Snopes
or a Rappler helps to provide citizens with that immediate feedback loop where they can
detect and debunk disinformation, but not the citizens, also journalists. We heard from folks
that it's important to be aware of some of the risks of fact-checking not being sustainable,
and so it's important to not only build this into the work of journalists but to ensure that it's a
part of the everyday. It's not a once-a-week operation. It's a daily operation because,
again, you're looking for quick feedback loops and instant debunking. The greatest advantage
of the fact-checking space and working through investigative journalists is that it is possible
to do this work in closed spaces, and if you are aware of the political economy in which you're
working, if you can identify neutral parties within government to partner with, then bringing
in the fact-checking piece to debunk information in a way that aligns with the objectives of
government partners, again, just grafts onto existing programming and doesn't require a
standalone undertaking. So that is the advocacy argument for fact-checking, and investigative
journalism. We hope you will support us. Awesome. Thank you, Lori, and again, we cannot
underestimate the importance of those communicators and journalists who are providing the truth to us.
Next, we're going to hear from Nader Ali from the DRT Center to make the closing argument on
platform accountability. Thanks. Thanks, Josh, and thanks to the group of folks that showed up and
especially to Amy for leading us through the discussion. The main points that emerged from
our conversation on platform accountability were, firstly, that there's no doubt that these
platforms are here to stay, and as we well know, they're an integral part of our lives more than
ever now that COVID-19 has accelerated the adoption of technology. As a group, we talked
about how to do better platform governance while protecting human rights and how the
examples of Myanmar and Bosnia showed the critical need for strong USD leadership at the mission and
embassy level if we're going to succeed where we are at AID working in the trenches. So we need
strong leadership, and we need collaboration with important international partners such as
the United Nations, at least in the examples that we had from Myanmar and Bosnia. There were some
field suggestions that were really to start working more across the interagency, include
the public policy team and the poll econ and military sections of the embassy, and to really
keep an eye out in the country for alternative propagandist platforms that are being set up.
There was a recommendation and response to take advantage of the innovation technology hub back
here in DC. To sum up, our global network of staff and partners is uniquely positioned to tackle
platform accountability. We outlined three ways that we're really well placed to respond.
One, we have connections in the field among the people who are seeing the real risks and reward
of these technologies. Secondly, we have connections in DC among the people who are
shaping public policy around the technology. And thirdly, we have connections in Silicon Valley
among the people who are developing these technologies. So finally, as users, we cannot
advocate our responsibility to hold these platforms accountable, to ensure that they
serve our democratic values. So if not us, then who? Let's put some weight behind platform
accountability. Thank you. Wow. Thank you, Nadira. And I really love this argument because
it really inscribes a very particular role that USAID is incredibly well placed to make a
difference. And so we should really be taking advantage of that. And then finally, last but not
least, Lisa Poggioli from Africa Bureau is going to talk about the Group on Messaging campaign.
Thanks, Josh. Hi, all. I'm just going to be on video for a second because I only have it on my
phone. So I'll go off now. But thanks, everyone who joined our messaging group. And thanks,
Adam, for being our fearless leader and giving the opening argument. So as Adam noted in his
opening argument, it is naive to believe we'll be able to fully stop or fully control disinformation.
But our group has concluded we can best mitigate its destructive effects through positive messaging
and content generation. As humans, we bond with others over stories and images. We make meaning
through telling our stories. Powerful messages move people. However, we know that not all messaging
and content creation is created equal. For it to be effective, we discussed that it has to be
thoughtful, targeted, and context-specific. So what does that mean? First, it means that messages
should focus on the values and ideas we want to promote, like freedom of expression, social
inclusion, and tolerance, but couch them in compelling stories and media forms that will
resonate with our target audience. So we discussed how this might mean thinking of messaging as a
locally targeted marketing or advertising campaign instead of a traditional strategic
communications campaign. It also might mean incorporating comedy, drama, and the arts into
messaging if those are locally popular modes of expression. Second, and relatedly, we discussed
that messages must be rooted in a strong understanding of the cultures of information
sharing in the context that we work in. So by cultures of information sharing, I'm talking about
the motivations that drive people to share information, the circumstances under which
they share information, the platforms and forms of media they use to share information, and the style
and substance of the information itself, including considerations like language, locally resonant
symbols, and images. And I'll note one recent example of research published in the International
Journal of Communication that shows that in sub-Saharan Africa, citizens often share made-up
news intentionally, and that they do so for two primary reasons, civic duty and fun. So on the
latter point, the researchers point out that in sub-Saharan African context, satire in the form of
comic strips or comedy shows has historically been an important alternative channel of information
when trust in mainstream media is low, and this is in large part because mainstream media has
historically been owned by the state and geared towards social elites in sub-Saharan Africa.
So if we understand this context in which sharing misinformation is viewed as entertainment,
we can employ a similar satirical style in our own messaging campaigns, which can help to build
trust with our target audiences and generate engagement. And messages are powerful in part
because sharing them is a means to build and maintain social bonds through trust. So what is
shared is not just news and information, but also a sign of trust between a sender and the recipient.
And so we're arguing that by creating messages that resonate and that are targeting,
we can not only counter disinformation, but also help to build trust, which has the potential to
generate positive development outcomes well beyond any one counter disinformation initiative.
And then finally, we noted that messaging does not need to be generated by us. And in fact,
designing programs for use in particular can generate their own content around the issues
they care about. And this is especially issues that communities circulate as different
disinformation is a great way to empower the communities we work with to engage in healthy
civic discourse and create alternatives to the damaging narratives that are unfortunately
saturating their online and frequently offline worlds. Thanks. Lisa, thank you so much for that.
And also what I really appreciate about the argument you've made is that there's a lot of
evidence to show us how to do this right. And we just need to pay attention to that evidence.
So we're about to close up the hour. And I just hope that you all had an opportunity to learn
from your colleagues. I know I learned a lot from my colleagues. I'm so honored to be working with
these colleagues, with all of you. And we're going to give you a second chance to vote on the
argument that really resonated with you. So Cheyenne's putting in another link into the polls,
if you look on the right hand side. And I just want to, you know, while you're voting,
I want to just give my thanks to all of those of you who spent an hour with us joining the
conversation in this collective opportunity to learn. I want to give special thanks to all of
our presenters, the advocates, and the rapporteurs who made these really compelling cases for the
work that we do and can do more of. And I think they all inspired us. And I also want to thank

a plug for the disinformation primer. There are more details and more resources for all of us to

is actually kind of fun, and I hope we do have fun moving forward. Regarding the primer, we really
are interested in getting your feedback. We're open to suggestions on how to improve the product
and have, we put out some questions in the follow-up survey to hear from you. So if you
have read it and you have some feedback, don't worry about any hurt feelings. We really want

just the fact that we have these kinds of discussions, that we're concerned about this issue,
is a good indicator that we're moving in the right direction on this issue. So please
await a follow-up survey from Sujin and Cheyenne. And again, I want to thank you all for taking
this time. And I guess we're going to see results from voting soon. And I just, one thing about the
voting, I just wanted to say, it doesn't really matter who gets more votes. It's, I'm kind of
interested in seeing, like, if there was a change in voting from the beginning to the end of this
session. But I think all of these, and even regardless, I think these are all legitimate
approaches and they all deserve more attention. We only gave you a tiny glimpse of them right now,
but I hope this inspires you to study them further. Thank you. Thank you. Thanks, Jerry.
